summaries.example: Think about a red toy ball. The ball is a thing you can hold, see, and move. Red and round describe how the ball is. Philosophers ask whether the ball and its properties—redness and roundness—belong to different basic groups.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of objects asks three big questions. First, are objects different from non-objects, such as properties, or is everything that exists an object? Second, which things belong in the group called objects? Ordinary examples include balls, books, trees, and boats, but philosophers may disagree about tiny particles, very large collections, or things made from parts. Third, what are objects like inside? One theory says an object is a bundle of properties. Another says it has properties plus a special basic part. A different family of theories says properties are not parts at all; objects simply stand in a relation to them. These debates show that a familiar word can hide difficult questions about reality.
key_ideas: Philosophers do not all mean the same thing by “object.” Some think every existing thing is an object.
Another view separates objects, such as trees and people, from properties, such as greenness and kindness.
Philosophers compare objects and properties in several ways: objects are usually in space and time, while properties may not be.
They also ask which things count as objects and what objects are made of.
Some theories say objects are bundles of properties. Other theories say properties are related to objects but are not parts of them.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use objects and their features every day, but deciding what really exists affects how we understand science, language, change, and identity. The topic also teaches an important philosophical habit: separate the question of what a word means from the question of what the world is like.

important_terms.definition: A thing or item, in a broad philosophical sense. Some philosophers use this word for nearly everything that exists.
A feature that something has, such as being red, heavy, or round.
A system for sorting things into very general groups, such as objects and properties.
The question of what things there are.

questions_to_think_about: Is a color an object, a property, or something else?
Could two objects have exactly the same properties and still be two objects?
Are all groups of parts together an object, or only some groups?
Can something be talked about or thought about without being an object?

summaries.example: Consider two perfectly similar spheres. They might share every ordinary property: the same color, shape, size, and mass. One debate asks whether sharing all properties would make them one object rather than two. The Identity of Indiscernibles would suggest that two things with exactly the same properties are identical, but many philosophers think two exactly similar objects are possible. This raises a further question: what makes each sphere a distinct object?
summaries.summary: The entry examines “object” as a possible ontological category. Its first question concerns contrast: are there non-objects, and are properties the main alternative? The Umbrella View says that every thing is an object, but this involves two independent ideas: a metaphysical thesis that reality has one fully general category and a semantic thesis about how the word “object” is used. If objects contrast with properties, philosophers have proposed several tests. Objects may be subjects of predication, located in space and time, wholly located in only one region, concrete, perceptible, and able to instantiate properties; properties may have the opposite features. None of these contrasts is presented as uncontroversial. A subject-object contrast supplies another use: subjects are experiencers, while objects may be things experienced. The entry then asks which things are objects—the extension question—and distinguishes it from the question of what exists. Nihilism, monism, and pluralism offer very different answers about existence, while the Special Composition Question asks when parts compose an object. Finally, theories of nature divide between constituent ontologies, in which properties are parts of objects, and relational ontologies, in which objects have properties through an external relation. Bundle theory, bare particularism, hylomorphism, Platonism, and class nominalism develop different versions of these ideas.
key_ideas: The debate over objects has three dimensions: contrast, extension, and nature.
The Umbrella View combines a claim about reality—a fully general category—with a claim about language: that “object” names it. These claims can be separated.

A leading contrast treats objects as particulars and properties as universals. Proposed differences involve subject-predicate structure, location in space and time, abstractness, perception, and instantiation.
The ontological question asks what exists, while the extension question asks which existing things are objects. They coincide on some theories but not on all.
Possible answers about existence include nihilism, monism, and pluralism. These positions differ over whether there are no objects, exactly one object, or more than one.
Theories of object nature include bundle theory, bare particularism, hylomorphism, and relational views. They disagree about whether properties are constituents of objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: The category of object is involved in ordinary thought, scientific explanation, logic, and metaphysical theories of parts and properties. Clarifying it prevents several questions from being confused: what a word means, what exists, which existing things count as objects, and what objects are. The debate also illustrates how broad philosophical categories can organize reality while remaining difficult to define.

important_terms.definition: A very general way of dividing reality, such as object, property, event, or entity.
The view that “object” names a maximally general category containing every thing that exists.
A feature or way something is, such as being tall, green, or kind; properties may be contrasted with objects.
The set of things that fall under a category; the extension of “object” is the things counted as objects.
The philosophical investigation of what exists and what kinds of things there are.
The principle that if two things share every property, they are identical; its application to objects is controversial.
The view that properties are parts or constituents of the objects that have them.
The question of when some things together compose another object.

questions_to_think_about: Could “object” be a useful category even if it includes everything?
Why might a philosopher distinguish a disagreement about a word from a disagreement about reality?
Does being in space and time successfully separate objects from properties?
What would make a collection of particles form one object rather than many?
Would a theory with fewer basic objects be preferable if it explained the same physical facts?

summaries.example: Imagine a set of identical-looking school notebooks. Each notebook is a separate physical item, but all may share the property of having the same shape. The notebooks are in different places, while the one shared shape seems to be present in many places at once. This gives one reason to distinguish objects from properties. Still, philosophers ask whether this difference is really fundamental, since we recognize the shared shape by looking at the notebooks that have it.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the philosophical category of object through three questions. The contrast question asks whether objects have a complement, such as properties, or whether everything belongs to the object category. The Umbrella View says that every thing is an object, but it combines a claim about a universal category with a claim about the use of a word; either claim could be considered separately. If objects are contrasted with properties, proposed differences include being subjects rather than predicates, existing in space and time, being wholly located in one place, being concrete and perceptible, and being able to have properties rather than be instantiated. These proposals are debated. A different contrast uses “object” for what is experienced, opposed to a conscious subject. The extension question asks which things count as objects, and the ontological question asks what exists; these questions may have different answers. The entry considers nihilism, monism, pluralism, and theories about composition. It ends with theories of nature: constituent views treat properties as parts of objects, whereas relational views treat having a property as a relation between an object and something outside it.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask whether “object” includes everything or contrasts with a group such as properties.
The Umbrella View contains both a claim about the world and a claim about the meaning of the word “object.” The two claims do not automatically prove each other.
Objects and properties have been compared by looking at language, location, concrete and abstract things, perception, and the relation of instantiation.
The question “What exists?” is not always the same as “Which things are objects?” A theory may accept properties or other non-objects.
Philosophers disagree about existence: some defend no objects, one object, or many objects.
Theories of object nature disagree about whether properties are internal parts of objects or are connected to objects by a relation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea of an object seems simple in everyday life, but it supports important questions about language, science, identity, and parts and wholes. Studying competing accounts helps us notice that philosophers may disagree not only about the answer, but also about which question should be asked first.

important_terms.definition: A very general group used to classify reality, such as object, property, event, or being.
The idea that everything that exists falls under the category of object, so object has no real opposite.
A feature something has, such as being blue, tall, or generous.
The things included in a category. The extension of object is whatever the theory counts as an object.
The study of what exists and how existing things are grouped.
The idea that properties can be shared by many objects, while each object is wholly in one place at a time.
A view that an object is made from properties or property-like parts.
The question of what conditions make several things become one larger thing.

questions_to_think_about: If every existing thing were an object, would the category still help us classify reality?
Can a property, such as a shape, be in several places at once?
What could make two objects different if they have all the same properties?
Should every group of connected parts count as an object?
Is something an object because it can be referred to, or can reference include non-objects too?
